title: Old-Time Vegetable Storage Pits
subtitle: 1917 USDA Wisdom
items: Leave a straw vent on top
desc: Old-time outdoor storage pits from USDA Farmers' Bulletin 879, Home Storage of Vegetables (1917), rewritten for today: on well-drained ground, pile carrots, beets, turnips or cabbage in a straw-lined cone, cover with straw and then soil, leave a straw vent at the top and dig a drainage ditch. Make several small pits and open one at a time. A no-cellar way to store root vegetables all winter.

title: How to Pressure Can Pumpkin
subtitle: USDA Tested: Cubes Only
desc: How to safely pressure can pumpkin and winter squash following the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning: peel, cut into 1-inch cubes, boil 2 minutes, hot pack with cooking liquid and 1-inch headspace, and process pints 55 minutes or quarts 90 minutes at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–1,000 ft) or 11 lb (dial gauge), adjusting for altitude. Never can mashed or pureed pumpkin; freeze puree instead.

title: How to Freeze Broccoli
subtitle: Blanch for Best Quality
desc: How to freeze fresh broccoli so it stays green and tasty: cut into even florets, soak in salt water to drive out garden worms, rinse, blanch 3 minutes in boiling water, chill in ice water, drain, then pack in freezer bags with the air pressed out. Easy food preservation for your fall garden harvest.

title: Keep Pipes From Freezing
subtitle: Winter Home Prep
desc: How to keep pipes from freezing this winter: disconnect and drain garden hoses, insulate pipes in crawl spaces and garages, open sink cabinets so warm air reaches the plumbing, let faucets drip during cold snaps, keep the heat at 55°F or higher even when away, and know where your main water shutoff is. Simple winter prep for a self-sufficient home.

title: Clean Garden Tools for Winter
subtitle: Make Them Last for Years
items: Scrub rust with a wire brush
desc: How to clean and store garden tools for winter: remove soil, scrub off rust with a wire brush, sharpen hoes, shovels and pruners, wipe metal with a light coat of oil, sand and oil wooden handles, and hang tools in a dry shed. A simple end-of-season task that gets your vegetable garden ready for spring.
